meta.note: Sample bank for the ABLE Preps SAT practice prototype. Every item is original. Tags follow the College Board Digital SAT domain/skill taxonomy so the bank can grow into it. Each item is reviewed by a person before it ships; nothing here is auto-generated at runtime.

Advanced Math: Systems of equations in two variables
Problem-Solving and Data Analysis: Ratios, rates, proportional relationships, and units
One-variable data: distributions and measures of center and spread
Inference from sample statistics and margin of error

questions.passage: Urban beekeeping has grown rapidly over the past decade. Cities such as Paris and Toronto now host thousands of hives on rooftops and in parks. Proponents argue that city bees often thrive because urban gardens offer a wide variety of flowers throughout the growing season, whereas bees in farming regions may face vast fields planted with a single crop.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Beekeeping in farming regions is declining because farms grow only one crop.
Urban beekeeping has expanded, in part because cities can offer bees a varied food supply.
Paris and Toronto have the largest bee populations of any cities in the world.
Bees kept in cities produce more honey than bees kept in the countryside.
questions.explanation: The text's first sentence introduces the growth of urban beekeeping, and the rest explains one reason for it: cities offer varied flowers. Choice B captures both. A overstates a comparison the text only hints at, C is not supported (the text says "thousands of hives," not the largest populations), and D is never claimed.

questions.passage: A researcher hypothesizes that people retain information better when they read it on paper than when they read the same material on a screen.
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researcher's hypothesis?
choices: Participants who read a passage on paper recalled more details in a later test than participants who read the same passage on a screen.
Participants reported that reading on paper felt more comfortable than reading on a screen.
Participants finished reading the passage more quickly on a screen than on paper.
Participants who read on a screen said afterward that they would have preferred paper.
questions.explanation: The hypothesis is about retention. Only choice A measures retention directly (recall on a later test) and compares the two formats. B and D are about preference, and C is about speed; none of those show that information was retained better.

questions.passage: Some historians have argued that the printing press caused a sudden rise in literacy in fifteenth-century Europe. Yet surviving records show that reading instruction remained rare for decades after presses appeared, and that most early printed books were purchased by institutions rather than by individuals. Taken together, these records suggest that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the printing press was adopted across Europe more slowly than historians have assumed.
the spread of literacy depended on factors beyond the availability of printed books.
institutions, not individuals, were the primary producers of early printed books.
reading instruction became widespread as soon as printed books became affordable.
questions.explanation: The evidence (instruction stayed rare; books went to institutions) undercuts the idea that presses alone drove literacy, which points to B. A is about the pace of adoption, which the text does not address. C confuses buyers with producers. D contradicts the text, which says instruction remained rare.

questions.passage: The committee's decision was far from ______: members debated for hours before reaching a narrow majority.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: unanimous
deliberate
temporary
predictable
questions.explanation: A "narrow majority" after hours of debate means the members did not all agree, so the decision was far from unanimous. "Deliberate" would actually fit a long debate, and nothing in the text concerns whether the decision was temporary or predictable.

questions.passage: Marine biologist Ana Ruiz spent three summers tagging sea turtles off the coast of Costa Rica. Her team's data revealed that the turtles returned to the same nesting beach each year with remarkable precision. Ruiz now hopes to determine how the animals navigate across thousands of miles of open ocean.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the third sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It presents a question raised by the findings described earlier in the text.
It summarizes the method the team used to gather its data.
It challenges the accuracy of the team's data.
It explains why the turtles prefer one particular beach.
questions.explanation: Sentences one and two describe the method and the finding; sentence three turns to what Ruiz wants to find out next, a question that the finding (precise return) raises. It does not summarize method (B), doubt the data (C), or explain the preference (D).

questions.passage:
Text 1

Many educators believe that homework builds discipline and reinforces classroom learning, and they point to studies showing a modest correlation between time spent on homework and grades among high school students.

Text 2

Psychologist Dana Cole notes that the correlation between homework and grades weakens or disappears among younger students. She argues that for elementary students, time spent on homework would be better spent on reading for pleasure and on unstructured play.
questions.stem: Based on the texts, how would Cole (Text 2) most likely respond to the educators described in Text 1?
choices: By arguing that homework should be eliminated at every grade level.
By noting that the benefits they cite may not apply to younger students.
By agreeing that homework improves grades for students of all ages.
By questioning whether discipline can be measured at all.
questions.explanation: Cole does not dispute the high school correlation; she points out it fades for younger students, which is B. A goes further than she does (she addresses elementary students only), C contradicts her, and D raises a point neither text makes.

questions.passage: The museum's new wing was designed to maximize natural light. ______ nearly every gallery has floor-to-ceiling windows.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: However,
Accordingly,
In contrast,
Nevertheless,
questions.explanation: The second sentence is a consequence of the design goal in the first, so a cause-and-effect transition fits: "Accordingly." The other three all signal contrast, which the sentences do not have.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• The Great Green Wall is a project to plant a belt of trees and restore land across Africa's Sahel region.
• It was launched in 2007 by the African Union.
• Its goal is to restore 100 million hectares of degraded land by 2030.
• As of 2023, roughly 18 million hectares had been restored.
• The project also aims to create millions of jobs.
questions.stem: The student wants to emphasize how much of the project's land-restoration goal remains unmet. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Launched in 2007, the Great Green Wall aims to restore land across Africa's Sahel region.
By 2023, the Great Green Wall had restored about 18 million hectares, less than a fifth of its 100-million-hectare goal.
The Great Green Wall is expected to create millions of jobs in the Sahel.
The African Union launched the Great Green Wall to restore 100 million hectares by 2030.
questions.explanation: Only B puts the progress (18 million) next to the goal (100 million) and states the gap, which is exactly what the student wants to emphasize. A, C, and D each state a fact from the notes but say nothing about how much remains.

questions.passage: The collection of essays, which spans three decades of the author's career, ______ readers a rare view of her evolving style.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: offer
offers
have offered
are offering
questions.explanation: The subject is the singular noun "collection" (not "essays," which sits inside the prepositional phrase "of essays"), so the verb must be singular: "offers."

questions.passage: Three elements make the bridge remarkable: its ______ its span, and its age.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: height;
height,
height:
height—
questions.explanation: The blank sits between the first and second items of a simple three-item list, which are separated by commas. Semicolons separate list items only when the items themselves contain commas; a colon or dash would wrongly break the list.

questions.passage: Originally scheduled for March, ______
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: the launch was pushed back to May by the engineering team.
the engineering team pushed the launch back to May.
May became the new date chosen by the engineering team.
the engineering team's plans for the launch were pushed back to May.
questions.explanation: The opening modifier "Originally scheduled for March" must describe the noun that follows it. Only the launch was scheduled for March, so "the launch" has to come right after the comma. B makes the team the scheduled thing, C makes May, and D makes the team's plans.

questions.passage: Although the novel was praised for its ambitious scope, some critics found its plot ______, noting that several storylines were introduced and then abandoned.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: cohesive
fragmented
conventional
restrained
questions.explanation: Storylines that are introduced and then abandoned make a plot broken into pieces: "fragmented." "Cohesive" is the opposite, and neither "conventional" nor "restrained" describes abandoned storylines.

questions.stem: If 3x + 7 = 22, what is the value of x?
questions.explanation: Subtract 7 from both sides: 3x = 15. Divide by 3: x = 5.

questions.stem: A gym charges a one-time membership fee of $40 plus $25 per month. Which equation gives the total cost C, in dollars, of a membership lasting m months?
choices: C = 65m
questions.explanation: The $40 is paid once, so it is the constant term. The $25 repeats each month, so it multiplies m: C = 40 + 25m. Choice A swaps the two amounts.

questions.stem:
The system of equations below has no solution. What is the value of k?

2x + 3y = 12
4x + ky = 20
questions.explanation: A system has no solution when the lines are parallel: same slope, different intercepts. Multiplying the first equation by 2 gives 4x + 6y = 24. For the second line to be parallel, its y-coefficient must match: k = 6. The constants differ (24 vs. 20), so the lines are distinct and never meet.

questions.stem: Which expression is equivalent to (x + 3)(x − 5)?
questions.explanation: Expand: x·x = x², x·(−5) = −5x, 3·x = 3x, 3·(−5) = −15. Combine the middle terms: −5x + 3x = −2x. Result: x² − 2x − 15.

questions.stem: The population of a town is 8,000 and increases by 5% each year. Which function models the population P(t) after t years?
questions.explanation: A 5% yearly increase multiplies the population by 1.05 each year, so after t years it is 8000 × 1.05ᵗ. Choice B multiplies by 0.05 (a 95% drop), C is linear rather than exponential, and D uses 50% growth.

questions.stem: The equation x² − 6x + c = 0 has exactly one real solution. What is the value of c?
questions.explanation: A quadratic has exactly one real solution when its discriminant is zero: b² − 4ac = 0. Here (−6)² − 4(1)(c) = 36 − 4c = 0, so c = 9. (Check: x² − 6x + 9 = (x − 3)², one solution at x = 3.)

questions.stem: A jacket originally priced at $80 is on sale for 25% off. What is the sale price of the jacket?
questions.explanation: 25% of $80 is $20, so the discount is $20 and the sale price is $80 − $20 = $60. Choice A is the discount itself, not the price.

questions.skill: Ratios, rates, proportional relationships, and units
questions.stem: A car travels 210 miles using 6 gallons of gasoline. At the same rate, how many gallons of gasoline are needed to travel 350 miles?
questions.explanation: The rate is 210 ÷ 6 = 35 miles per gallon. For 350 miles: 350 ÷ 35 = 10 gallons. Equivalently, set up the proportion 210/6 = 350/g and solve for g.

questions.skill: One-variable data: distributions and measures of center and spread
questions.stem: The mean of a list of five numbers is 12. When a sixth number is added to the list, the mean of the six numbers is 14. What is the sixth number?
questions.explanation: Mean × count = total. Five numbers with mean 12 total 5 × 12 = 60. Six numbers with mean 14 total 6 × 14 = 84. The sixth number is the difference: 84 − 60 = 24.

questions.stem: A rectangle has a length of 12 centimeters and a width of 5 centimeters. What is the area of the rectangle, in square centimeters?
questions.explanation: Area of a rectangle = length × width = 12 × 5 = 60. Choice A is the sum of the sides and B is the perimeter.

questions.stem: A right triangle has legs of length 9 and 12. What is the length of the hypotenuse?
questions.explanation: By the Pythagorean theorem, hypotenuse² = 9² + 12² = 81 + 144 = 225, so the hypotenuse is √225 = 15. (This is the 3-4-5 triangle scaled by 3.)

questions.stem: A circle in the xy-plane has the equation x² + y² − 6x + 4y = 12. What is the radius of the circle?
questions.explanation: Complete the square for each variable. x² − 6x becomes (x − 3)² − 9, and y² + 4y becomes (y + 2)² − 4. So (x − 3)² + (y + 2)² − 13 = 12, giving (x − 3)² + (y + 2)² = 25. The radius is √25 = 5; choice D is the radius squared.

questions.passage: In a 2019 survey of 40 city blocks, researchers found that blocks with mature street trees had summer surface temperatures up to 6°C lower than blocks without them. The effect was strongest where tree canopy covered at least 40 percent of the sidewalk. The researchers caution, however, that newly planted saplings provide little cooling during their first decade.
questions.stem: According to the text, what did the researchers find about newly planted saplings?
choices: They lower surface temperatures as effectively as mature trees do.
They provide little cooling for roughly their first ten years.
They survive best on blocks with at least 40 percent canopy cover.
They raise surface temperatures on the blocks where they are planted.
questions.explanation: The last sentence states directly that saplings "provide little cooling during their first decade," which is choice B. A contradicts that sentence, C connects two details the text never links, and D is not stated anywhere.

questions.passage:
Tutoring hours by volunteer, fall semester

Volunteer   Sept   Oct   Nov
Ana          12     15    18
Ben          20     14     9
Chloe         8      8     8
Dev           5     11    17

A student reviewing the table claims that one volunteer's tutoring hours declined every month.
questions.stem: Which choice best supports the student's claim?
choices: Ana tutored 12 hours in September and 18 hours in November.
Ben tutored 20 hours in September, 14 in October, and 9 in November.
Chloe tutored 8 hours in each of the three months.
Dev tutored more hours in November than in September.
questions.explanation: The claim needs a volunteer whose hours drop from each month to the next. Only Ben's do: 20, then 14, then 9. Ana and Dev increase, and Chloe stays flat.

questions.passage: Coral reefs depend on a partnership with tiny algae that live inside the coral and supply it with most of its food. When ocean water becomes too warm, corals expel the algae and turn white, a process called bleaching. Bleached corals are not dead, but because they have lost their main food source, ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: they recover fully as soon as the water temperature changes.
they can starve if the water does not cool soon enough for the algae to return.
they begin producing their own food instead.
they no longer depend on the surrounding water.
questions.explanation: The setup is that the algae supply most of the coral's food and bleaching means losing them. The logical consequence is that a bleached coral risks starving unless the algae come back, which is B. A ignores the food problem, and C and D contradict the dependence the text establishes.

questions.passage: Most people picture a desert as endless sand. In fact, only about a quarter of the Sahara is sand dunes; the rest is gravel plains, rocky plateaus, and salt flats.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It presents a common assumption and then corrects it.
It describes a problem and then proposes a solution.
It lists several deserts in order of size.
It explains the process by which deserts form.
questions.explanation: "Most people picture..." sets up the assumption; "In fact..." corrects it with the real makeup of the Sahara. No problem or solution is raised, no other deserts are named, and formation is never discussed.

questions.passage:
Text 1

Scholars have long attributed the anonymous fourteenth-century poem to a single author, pointing to its consistent style and unified structure.

Text 2

Linguist Mara Feld analyzed the poem's vocabulary and found two distinct dialect patterns concentrated in different sections. She argues that this distribution is difficult to explain if only one person wrote the poem.
questions.stem: Based on the texts, how would Feld (Text 2) most likely respond to the scholars described in Text 1?
choices: By agreeing that the poem's unified structure proves a single author wrote it.
By suggesting that consistency of style does not rule out more than one author.
By arguing that the poem was written after the fourteenth century.
By claiming that the poem has no unified structure at all.
questions.explanation: Feld's evidence (two dialect patterns) points toward multiple authors even though the style is consistent, so she would say consistency alone does not settle the question: B. She does not dispute the structure (D) or the date (C), and A is the opposite of her position.

questions.passage: Solar panels have become far cheaper over the past decade. ______ many homeowners still hesitate to install them because of the upfront cost.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: As a result,
Similarly,
Even so,
For example,
questions.explanation: The second sentence runs against what the first would lead you to expect (cheaper panels, yet hesitation), so a concessive transition is needed: "Even so." "As a result" would claim the hesitation follows from the price drop, and the other two do not signal contrast.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Wangari Maathai was a Kenyan environmental activist.
• In 1977 she founded the Green Belt Movement.
• The movement paid rural women to plant trees.
• By 2004 the movement had planted more than 30 million trees.
• In 2004 Maathai became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.
questions.stem: The student wants to convey the scale of the Green Belt Movement to an audience unfamiliar with Maathai. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Wangari Maathai won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2004.
Kenyan activist Wangari Maathai's Green Belt Movement, founded in 1977, had planted more than 30 million trees by 2004.
The Green Belt Movement paid rural women to plant trees.
Maathai, the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize, founded a movement.
questions.explanation: The audience needs to be told who Maathai is (Kenyan activist) and given the scale (30 million trees). Only B does both. A and D are about the prize, not the movement's scale, and C describes the method without any numbers.

questions.passage: The observatory's telescope, which was installed in ______ remains one of the largest of its kind.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: "which was installed in 1962" is a nonessential clause opened by a comma after "telescope," so it must be closed by a matching comma. A semicolon or colon would break the sentence, and leaving the clause unclosed is also wrong.

questions.passage: The kit includes everything a beginner ______ a board, a set of pieces, and an instruction booklet.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: needs,
needs;
needs:
needs
questions.explanation: What follows the blank is a list that explains "everything a beginner needs," and it is not an independent clause. A colon introduces such a list. A semicolon requires an independent clause on both sides, and a comma or nothing would run the list into the sentence.

questions.passage: By the time the rescue team arrived, the hikers ______ two nights on the ridge.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: spend
have spent
had spent
will spend
questions.explanation: "By the time the rescue team arrived" places one past event before another past event, which calls for the past perfect: "had spent." The other tenses do not sit before a past arrival.

questions.stem: The line y = 2x − 3 passes through the point (4, k). What is the value of k?
questions.explanation: Substitute x = 4: y = 2(4) − 3 = 8 − 3 = 5. So k = 5.

questions.stem: Which of the following values of x satisfies the inequality 4x − 5 > 11?
questions.explanation: Add 5 to both sides: 4x > 16. Divide by 4: x > 4. The only choice greater than 4 is 5. Note that 4 itself does not work, since the inequality is strict.

questions.stem: A scatterplot shows the relationship between the number of hours per day a plant is exposed to sunlight, s, and its height, h, in centimeters. The line of best fit is h = 3.2s + 4. According to the model, what is the predicted increase in height for each additional hour of daily sunlight?
choices: 3.2 cm
4 cm
7.2 cm
questions.explanation: In h = 3.2s + 4, the slope 3.2 is the change in h for each 1-unit increase in s. The 4 is the predicted height with zero sunlight (the intercept), not a rate.

questions.stem: A bag contains 5 red marbles, 3 blue marbles, and 2 green marbles. If one marble is selected at random, what is the probability that it is not red?
questions.explanation: There are 10 marbles in all and 5 are not red (3 blue + 2 green), so the probability is 5/10 = 1/2. Equivalently, 1 − P(red) = 1 − 5/10.

questions.stem: Two angles of a triangle measure 35° and 65°. What is the measure, in degrees, of the third angle?
questions.explanation: The angles of a triangle sum to 180°: 180 − 35 − 65 = 80.

questions.skill: Systems of equations in two variables
questions.stem: The graphs of y = x² and y = 2x + 3 intersect at two points. What is the sum of the x-coordinates of those points?
questions.explanation: Set the equations equal: x² = 2x + 3, so x² − 2x − 3 = 0, which factors as (x − 3)(x + 1) = 0. The x-coordinates are 3 and −1, and their sum is 2. (Shortcut: for x² + bx + c = 0 the roots sum to −b, here 2.)

questions.skill: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error
questions.stem: A random sample of 400 students at a school with 2,000 students found that 30% of the sample walk to school. Based on the sample, which of the following is the best estimate of the number of students at the school who walk to school?
questions.explanation: A random sample lets you apply its proportion to the whole population: 30% of 2,000 = 600. Choice A applies 30% to the sample instead of the school.

questions.skill: Ratios, rates, proportional relationships, and units
questions.stem: A recipe uses 3 cups of flour for every 2 cups of sugar. How many cups of flour are needed for 8 cups of sugar?
questions.explanation: Set up the proportion 3/2 = f/8. Cross-multiply: 2f = 24, so f = 12. Or notice 8 cups of sugar is 4 times the recipe, so 4 × 3 = 12 cups of flour.

questions.stem: The function f is defined by f(x) = x² − 4x + 7. What is the minimum value of f(x)?
questions.explanation: The parabola opens upward, so its minimum is at the vertex, x = −b/(2a) = 4/2 = 2. Then f(2) = 4 − 8 + 7 = 3. Choice B is the x-coordinate of the vertex, not the minimum value.

questions.stem: The price of an item is increased by 20%, and then the new price is decreased by 20%. The final price is what percent of the original price?
questions.explanation: Multiply the factors: 1.20 × 0.80 = 0.96, so the final price is 96% of the original. The percentages do not cancel because the 20% decrease is taken from a larger number than the 20% increase was added to.

questions.stem: A right circular cylinder has a radius of 3 and a height of 10. What is the volume of the cylinder?
questions.explanation: Volume of a cylinder = πr²h = π(3²)(10) = π(9)(10) = 90π.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to determine whether a new fertilizer causes tomato plants to grow taller. Which study design best supports a cause-and-effect conclusion?
choices: Survey gardeners who chose to use the fertilizer about their plants' heights.
Randomly assign tomato plants to receive either the fertilizer or no fertilizer, then compare the heights.
Measure the tallest plants in a garden that uses the fertilizer.
Compare plant heights in two gardens that already differ in whether they use the fertilizer.
questions.explanation: Only random assignment to treatment and control groups supports a cause-and-effect conclusion, because it spreads other differences evenly between the groups. The other designs are observational: the gardens or gardeners chose the fertilizer themselves, so anything else about them could explain a height difference.
